questions.question: Describe Rene Descartes' method of doubt and its importance. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Descartes proposed systematic skepticism—doubting everything that can possibly be doubted
  • (including the senses and external world) to find an absolutely certain foundation of knowledge.
  • This led to the famous conclusion “Cogito, ergo sum” (“I think, therefore I am”), which he
  • considered indubitable truth- The method of doubt laid the foundation for modern philosophy by
  • emphasizing reason and critical inquiry.

questions.question: How Gender relates to Witch Hunt? / [CO2, CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Gendered Targeting of Women: Witch-hunts disproportionately targeted women, especially
  • those who were socially marginal (widows, elderly, or independent women). Cultural beliefs
  • associated women with emotional instability, sexuality, and moral weakness, making them more
  • vulnerable to accusations of witchcraft- Reinforcement of Patriarchal Control:Witch-hunts
  • functioned as a mechanism to discipline and control women who deviated from accepted gender
  • roles. By punishing “deviant” behavior, societies reinforced patriarchal norms and limited
  • women’s autonomy and social power.

questions.question: Identify the relationship between unity and differentiation in science. / [CO1, CO3]
questions.solution_html:

  • empirical observation, experimentation, and the search for universal laws that explain natural
  • phenomena- Differentiation within Science: At the same time, science is differentiated into
  • specialized disciplines (e.g., physics, biology, chemistry), each focusing on specific domains,
  • methods, and levels of analysis, reflecting the complexity and diversity of knowledge.

questions.question: Analyse the contribution of Jesuit scholars to Early Modern Science. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Global Knowledge Networks-Jesuit scholars created extensive international networks
  • (Europe, Asia, Americas) that facilitated the exchange of scientific knowledge, especially in
  • astronomy, geography, and natural history-Advancement of Astronomy and Mathematics-
  • Figures like Christopher Clavius contributed to calendar reform (Gregorian calendar) and
  • promoted mathematical sciences within education and research-Science through Missionary
  • Work-Jesuits such as Matteo Ricci introduced European scientific ideas (astronomy,
  • cartography) to China while also bringing back indigenous knowledge to Europe-Educational
  • Institutions and Scientific Training-Jesuits established colleges and universities across Europe
  • that emphasized rigorous training in mathematics, natural philosophy, and experimental
  • methods-Mediation between Science and Religion-Jesuit scholars played a key role in
  • reconciling scientific discoveries with Catholic doctrine, engaging with debates around
  • heliocentrism and natural philosophy during the early modern period.

questions.question: Explain the importance of scientific societies and journals in spreading new scientific ideas and assess their impact on knowledge production. / [CO1, CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Institutional platforms for knowledge exchange-Scientific societies like the Royal Society
  • created formal spaces for scholars to meet, debate, and present findings, helping transform
  • science into a collective and organized activity-Dissemination through journals-Journals such as
  • the Philosophical Transactions enabled rapid circulation of new discoveries across regions,
  • making scientific knowledge more accessible and less dependent on personal networks-
  • Standardization and validation of knowledge-These institutions introduced practices like peer
  • evaluation and replication, which helped establish credibility, accuracy, and uniform methods in
  • knowledge production-Creation of scientific communities and networks-They connected
  • scientists across countries, fostering collaboration, cross-cultural exchange, and the emergence of
  • an international scientific community-Transformation of knowledge production-Scientific
  • societies and journals shifted knowledge production from isolated individuals to a collective,
  • cumulative, and institutional process, accelerating innovation and laying the foundation for
  • modern “Big Science.”

questions.question: 30. Discuss the health hazards caused by the Industrial Revolution. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Air and Environmental Pollution-Rapid industrialization led to heavy smoke, coal dust, and
  • toxic emissions, causing respiratory diseases such as bronchitis and asthma-Poor Working
  • Conditions-Factory workers were exposed to dangerous machinery, long hours, and unsafe
  • environments, resulting in frequent injuries, accidents, and occupational illnesses-Urban
  • Overcrowding and Sanitation Issues-Mass migration to industrial cities created slums with
  • inadequate housing, poor drainage, and lack of clean water, leading to diseases like cholera and
  • typhoid-Child and Women Labour Exploitation-Children and women worked in hazardous
  • conditions with little protection, causing physical deformities, fatigue, and long-term health
  • problems-Spread of Epidemics and Public Health Crises-Unsanitary living and working
  • conditions contributed to frequent outbreaks of infectious diseases, increasing mortality rates in
  • industrial towns.

questions.question: Discuss the contributions of Rene Descartes. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Father of Modern Philosophy-Descartes emphasized reason and doubt as the basis of
  • knowledge, marking a shift from medieval scholasticism to modern philosophy-Method of
  • Doubt-He introduced systematic skepticism—questioning all beliefs to arrive at certain truth,
  • famously expressed as “Cogito, ergo sum” (“I think, therefore I am”)-Development of Analytical
  • Geometry-Descartes linked algebra and geometry, creating the Cartesian coordinate system,
  • which became fundamental to modern mathematics-Mind–Body Dualism-He proposed that mind
  • and body are distinct substances, influencing later debates in philosophy, psychology, and
  • science-Contribution to Scientific Method-Descartes advocated a rational, mathematical
  • approach to science, helping shape the development of modern scientific thinking.

questions.question: How do you understand Michel Foucault’s concept of power? / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Power is Diffuse and Everywhere-Power is not concentrated in a single authority (like the
  • state) but is spread across society and exercised through everyday relationships and practices-
  • Power and Knowledge are Interlinked-Power produces knowledge and vice versa
  • (“power/knowledge”). What counts as truth is shaped by power structures, such as institutions
  • and discourses-Power is Productive, Not Just Repressive-Power does not only repress or control;
  • it also creates realities, identities, norms, and forms of behavior (e.g., shaping what is considered
  • “normal”)-Power Operates through Discourses-Systems of thought (discourses) define and
  • regulate knowledge, influencing how people think, speak, and understand the world-Power is
  • Relational and Dynamic-Power exists in relationships and is constantly shifting; where there is
  • power, there is also resistance, making it fluid rather than fixed.

questions.question: Give a brief account of Samir Amin’s critique of Eurocentrism. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Eurocentrism as Ideology-Amin argues that Eurocentrism is not neutral knowledge but an
  • ideological construct that presents Europe as the center and driver of world history-False
  • Universalism-It falsely universalizes European historical experiences (like capitalism and
  • modernity) as a model for all societies, ignoring diverse developmental paths-Distortion of
  • Global History-Eurocentrism marginalizes and undervalues contributions of non-European
  • civilizations, especially in Asia and Africa, to science, culture, and economy-Justification of
  • Capitalist Domination-Amin links Eurocentrism to global capitalism, arguing it legitimizes
  • imperialism, colonialism, and unequal development between the “core” and “periphery.”-Call for
  • Delinking and Plurality-He advocates “delinking” from Eurocentric models and emphasizes the
  • need for alternative, plural paths of development rooted in local histories and conditions.

questions.question: Describe the socio-political background of hybrid scientific practices. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Colonial encounters and knowledge exchange-Hybrid scientific practices emerged in colonial
  • contexts where European science interacted with indigenous knowledge systems. Colonial
  • administrations depended on local expertise (e.g., in medicine, agriculture), leading to blended
  • forms of knowledge rather than pure imposition-Power, hierarchy, and epistemic dominance-
  • Scientific hybridity was shaped by unequal power relations—Western science was often
  • privileged as “universal,” while local knowledge was subordinated, yet still selectively
  • incorporated, producing hybrid forms under asymmetrical authority-Role of intermediaries and
  • knowledge brokers-Translators, native informants, missionaries, and local elites mediated
  • between knowledge systems. These actors played a crucial role in adapting, translating, and
  • reshaping scientific ideas across cultural boundaries-Institutional settings and state interests-
  • Colonial institutions (botanical gardens, surveys, medical colleges) encouraged hybridization to
  • serve administrative needs like resource extraction, governance, and public health, blending
  • empirical local practices with European frameworks-Resistance, adaptation, and localization-
  • Indigenous communities and practitioners did not passively accept Western science; they
  • adapted, resisted, and reinterpreted it. This resulted in localized, hybrid scientific practices
  • reflecting both global influences and local priorities.

  • Rational-It aims to be objective, logical, and free from personal bias, using reasoning and critical
  • thinking to explain phenomena-Dynamic and Evolving-Scientific knowledge is not fixed; it

questions.question: Apply the idea of specialization to explain the emergence of new scientific fields. / [CO4] [5x6 = 30]
questions.solution_html:
• Division of Knowledge-As scientific knowledge expanded, it became too vast for one person
  • to master, leading to specialization into narrower areas of study- Depth over
  • Breadth:Specialization allowed scientists to focus deeply on specific problems, resulting in the
  • development of distinct disciplines (e.g., physics, chemistry, biology)-Emergence of Sub-
  • disciplines: Within existing sciences, further specialization created new fields (e.g., molecular
  • biology, astrophysics) based on refined methods and topics-Technological Advancement: New

  • encouraging the formation of new scientific areas-Institutional Support: Universities, research
  • institutes, and journals began organizing around specialized fields, reinforcing their identity and
  • promoting further growth.

questions.question: Evaluate the impact of Galileo's experimental mathematical approach on the scinetific revolution, while explaining its long term influence on later scientists. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Impact of Galileo’s Experimental–Mathematical Approach & Its Long-Term Influence
  • Fusion of Experiment and Mathematics-Galileo Galilei combined systematic experimentation
  • with mathematical formulation, establishing a new method for studying nature-Shift from
  • Qualitative to Quantitative Science-Replaced Aristotelian qualitative explanations with
  • measurable, numerical analysis of physical phenomena-Foundation of Modern Physics-His work
  • on motion (falling bodies, inertia) laid the groundwork for classical mechanics-Validation of
  • Controlled Experimentation-Emphasized repeatable experiments (e.g., inclined plane studies),
  • making empirical verification central to science-Challenge to Authority and Tradition-
  • Undermined reliance on ancient authorities like Aristotle, promoting independent inquiry-
  • Support for Heliocentrism-Provided observational evidence for Nicolaus Copernicus’s theory,
  • strengthening the scientific revolution-Influence on Newtonian Synthesis-Inspired Isaac Newton,
  • whose laws of motion and gravitation built directly on Galileo’s mathematical treatment of
  • motion-Standardization of Scientific Method-Helped shape the modern scientific method:
  • hypothesis → experiment → mathematical analysis → conclusion-Technological and
  • Instrumental Advancement-Improved use of instruments like the telescope, encouraging
  • precision and innovation in scientific tools-Long-term Legacy Across Sciences-His approach
  • influenced later scientists across disciplines, embedding mathematization and experimentation as
  • core principles of modern science.

questions.question: Examine the role of rationalisation in shaping modern scientific knowledge. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Emphasis on Reason over Tradition-Rationalisation prioritizes logic and reason instead of
  • religious beliefs or traditional authority, forming the basis of modern scientific inquiry-
  • Systematic Methodology-It promotes structured methods like observation, experimentation, and
  • verification, leading to standardized scientific practices-Quantification and Measurement-Reality
  • is increasingly understood through numbers, measurement, and mathematical models, enhancing
  • precision and objectivity-Objectivity and Neutrality-Rationalisation encourages detachment from
  • personal biases, aiming for universal and objective scientific truths-Disenchantment of Nature-
  • Nature is no longer seen as mystical but as governed by laws that can be discovered and
  • explained scientifically-Development of Scientific Laws-It enables the formulation of general
  • laws (e.g., laws of motion, thermodynamics) that explain natural phenomena predictably-
  • Specialisation and Differentiation-Rationalisation leads to the division of science into specialized
  • disciplines, increasing depth and expertise-Institutionalisation of Science-Scientific research
  • becomes organized within universities, laboratories, and professional bodies, ensuring systematic
  • knowledge production-Technological Advancement-Rational thinking drives innovation, linking
  • science with technology and industrial development-Bureaucratisation of Knowledge-Scientific
  • work becomes regulated, documented, and standardized, often guided by formal procedures and
  • peer review systems.

questions.question: Discuss vernacularization of science in colonies. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Meaning of Vernacularisation-Refers to the translation and adaptation of scientific knowledge
  • from European languages into local (vernacular) languages in colonial societies-Colonial
  • Context-Initiated under colonial rule to make Western science accessible to local populations,
  • often for administrative, educational, and missionary purposes-Role of Translation-Scientific
  • texts were translated into regional languages (e.g., Bengali, Tamil, Hindi), enabling wider
  • dissemination beyond elite, English-educated groups-Mediating Knowledge Systems-
  • Vernacularisation acted as a bridge between Western scientific ideas and indigenous knowledge
  • traditions, sometimes blending the two-Educational Reforms-Colonial governments and
  • missionaries introduced vernacular science education in schools to expand literacy and technical
  • skills among the masses-Print Culture and Publishing-Growth of printing presses and vernacular
  • journals helped circulate scientific ideas more widely in colonial societies-Creation of New
  • Terminology-Local languages developed new scientific vocabularies, often by borrowing,
  • adapting, or inventing terms to express modern concepts-Agency of Indigenous Intellectuals-
  • Local scholars, teachers, and reformers actively participated in translating, interpreting, and
  • reshaping scientific knowledge-Selective Adaptation and Resistance-Not all Western science
  • was accepted wholesale; local communities sometimes resisted or reinterpreted ideas based on
  • cultural beliefs-Long-term Impact-Contributed to the democratization of knowledge, growth of
  • scientific awareness, and the eventual rise of nationalist movements that linked science with
  • progress and self-reliance.

questions.question: Analyse the historical process behind the formation of scientific disciplines in the nineteenth century. / [CO2] [10x2 = 20]
questions.solution_html:
• Rise of Specialisation-Knowledge expanded rapidly, leading to division into distinct fields
  • (e.g., physics, chemistry, biology), replacing the earlier unified “natural philosophy.”-
  • Institutionalisation of Science-Universities and research institutes formalised disciplines through
  • dedicated departments, chairs, and laboratories-Professionalisation of Scientists-Science became
  • a full-time career with training, qualifications, and recognition, replacing amateur naturalists-
  • Development of Scientific Societies-Organisations like the Royal Society promoted disciplinary
  • boundaries through meetings, funding, and collaboration-Growth of Scientific Journals-
  • Specialised journals emerged, allowing discipline-specific communication and standardisation of
  • knowledge-Impact of Industrial Revolution-Industrial needs (engineering, chemistry, metallurgy)
  • pushed applied sciences to develop as independent disciplines-Laboratory-based Research-The
  • shift to experimental, lab-based science (e.g., in chemistry and physics) strengthened disciplinary
  • identity-Standardisation of Methods and Terminology-Each discipline developed its own
  • methods, tools, and vocabulary, distinguishing it from others-State and Patronage Support-
  • Governments funded scientific research for military, economic, and administrative purposes,
  • reinforcing specialised fields-Epistemological Differentiation-Thinkers like Auguste Comte
  • classified sciences hierarchically, legitimising their separation into distinct disciplines.
